summary: Specifies the MTU and frame format for sending IPv6 packets over Token Ring networks. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Token Ring was a network where a special token passed around a circle and only the holder could send. This says how to wrap IPv6 packets for it.

questions: how is ipv6 carried over token ring
how is ipv6 sent over token ring
what is the default ipv6 mtu on token ring
how are ipv6 multicast addresses mapped on token ring
subtitle: How IPv6 packets are framed, addressed and multicast on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a defined way to ride on Token Ring: which frame to use, what MTU to assume, how to form addresses, and how to map multicast onto a ring that has no Ethernet-style multicast.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets travel in LLC/SNAP frames with EtherType 0x86DD. Interface identifiers come from the 48-bit hardware address, and multicast addresses map to Token Ring functional addresses.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8064. It also warns implementors about Token Ring's non-canonical address bit order.

today: RFC 2470 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8064; it has not been obsoleted. Read it together with that update.

sections.title: What This Memo Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2470 specifies how IPv6 is carried over Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) networks. It covers four things: the MTU and frame format, how to form link-local addresses, and the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Redirect, Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages.

Implementors get one warning up front. Token Ring adaptors assume addresses are in non-canonical rather than canonical bit order, so addresses must be handled with special care. The RFC points to RFC 2469 for details. The document uses the RFC 2119 key words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) in their usual sense.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook for sending IPv6 mail around a Token Ring: what size the envelope is, what goes on the label, and how to write the address.

sections.title: Choosing the MTU
sections.content:
A Token Ring frame can only be as big as the time a node may hold the token allows. That time depends on the signaling rate and the number of nodes on the ring, so the maximum frame size varies. Implementations must therefore rely on manual configuration or router advertisements to learn the real MTU. Common defaults include approximately 2000, 4000 and 8000 octets.

With no other information, an implementation should use a default MTU of 1500 octets. That is compatible with all common 802.5 defaults and with Ethernet LANs behind transparent bridging.

With source route bridging, the path discovery to a neighbor can also reveal the MTU. The largest frame (LF) subfield of the routing information field limits the information field, which holds both the LLC header and the IPv6 datagram. The LLC header is always 8 octets for IPv6, so the IPv6 MTU is the LF frame size minus 8. A node that does this must keep a separate MTU for each neighbor. Some 802.1D LF values give an IP MTU below 1280, which is under the IPv6 minimum, so IPv6 communication over such paths is generally not possible.

When sources disagree, the priority order is: LF values from source route bridging (only for specific unicast destinations, and only if not greater than any router advertisement), then router advertisements (only if not greater than manual configuration), then manual configuration including DHCP, then the default of 1500.
sections.plainLanguage: How big an envelope fits depends on how long you may hold the baton. If nobody tells you, assume a medium size, 1500, that fits almost every ring.

sections.title: The Frame Format
sections.content:
IPv6 packets are sent in LLC/SNAP frames. After the Token Ring header (Starting Delimiter, Access Control, Frame Control, 48-bit destination and source addresses) comes the LLC/SNAP header, then the IPv6 header and payload, then the Frame Check Sequence, Ending Delimiter and Frame Status.

The LLC/SNAP fields have fixed values: DSAP and SSAP are 0xAA, the control field is 0x03 (Unnumbered Information), the OUI is 0x000000 (EtherType encoding), and the EtherType is 0x86DD for IPv6.

On bridged rings a routing information field (RIF) may follow the source address. It is present when the most significant bit of the source address is set to one. The RIF holds a two-octet Routing Control header followed by zero to seven two-octet Route Designators, each a (bridge, LAN segment) pair. Sending the sequence for specifically routed frames, that is unicast IP datagrams, is the sender's job.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPv6 packet goes in a standard envelope with a fixed stamp, 0x86DD, that says it is IPv6. On a ring with bridges, the sender may also write the route to follow on the front.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The Interface Identifier is built from an EUI-64 derived from the interface's built-in 48-bit address. The first three octets (the OUI) become the company_id. The fourth and fifth octets are set to FFFE. The last three octets of the Token Ring address become the last three of the EUI-64. Then the Universal/Local bit, the next-to-lowest bit of the first octet, is complemented.

The RFC's example: a built-in address of 34-56-78-9A-BC-DE in canonical bit order gives the identifier 36-56-78-FF-FE-9A-BC-DE. An address set manually or by software should not be used to derive the identifier. A prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration on Token Ring must be 64 bits long.

The link-local address is the Interface Identifier appended to the prefix FE80::/64.
sections.plainLanguage: Your IPv6 name tag is made from the serial number printed on your network card, with a few fixed digits stuffed in the middle and one bit flipped.

sections.title: Address Mapping for Unicast and Multicast
sections.content:
Unicast mapping follows Neighbor Discovery (RFC 2461). The Source/Target Link-layer Address option has Type 1 (source) or 2 (target), Length 1 (in units of 8 octets), and the 48-bit Token Ring address in canonical bit order. That is the address the interface currently responds to, which may differ from the built-in address used for the identifier. With source route bridges, the source route can be taken from the RIF of received Neighbor Advertisements, and a received RIF can be reversed for return traffic by toggling the D bit and making sure the frame is marked specifically routed.

All IPv6 multicast packets go to Token Ring functional addresses. All-nodes and solicited-node addresses share one functional address, all-routers has another, and every other multicast address maps by its three least significant bits to one of eight more. Other protocols may use these same functional addresses, so a frame sent there is not guaranteed to be IPv6.

In a bridged ring, all multicast packets SHOULD be sent with a RIF specifying the Spanning Tree Explorer. Some very old bridges are believed not to support this, so an implementation MAY allow an All Routes Explorer instead, but only if an administrator configures it. The default MUST be the Spanning Tree Explorer.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a neighbor's card number you ask on the ring. To shout to a group, you use special group mailboxes, and the group you shout to depends on the kind of message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is short. Token Ring, like most broadcast LAN technologies, has inherent vulnerabilities. For example, any sender can claim the identity of another and forge traffic. The RFC leaves it to higher layers to take appropriate steps where such vulnerabilities are unacceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: On a shared ring anyone can pretend to be someone else, so serious secrets need extra locks added on top.
